I joined to check controls. I left knowing how to question them, and how to turn the answer into change.

Ahmad Hassan, Portfolio of Professional Practice. Twelve months across two Chief Controls Offices at Lloyds Banking Group, from June 2025 to June 2026.

I spent my placement in two rotations in two different Chief Controls Offices: Incident Management first, then Control Design and Optimisation, where I worked mainly on IT systems risk. The high point came in January, when my team’s winning proposition took me to the Group COO and CTO. The year ended with a setback: I was not put forward for the graduate programme. Both are in here, along with what I did about the second one and how I will carry it into a graduate role.

How to read this

The chapters run in the order things happened, from my first week in June 2025 to my graduate applications in October 2026. Each one opens with the skills it shows, in the module’s own wording, and closes with what I learned and where I used it next.

Exhibits are numbered by chapter, and every reference in the text links to its exhibit. The progress bars are my own rating of my tools at that point in the year.

Colour shows which of the module’s five criteria areas a chapter mainly evidences. Every skill tag carries the colour of its area.

Choose an area to list every page and criterion where it is evidenced.

A note on the evidence

A Lloyds laptop cannot send anything to an email address outside the bank, so no working document left Lloyds with me. That is why every chart and table here is recreated with dummy data and labelled as such. To get my feedback in writing, I asked my line manager privately, and the PA to the director of the Chief Controls Office sent it to me, as one of the few people allowed to email outside the bank.

2Where I worked

Context for the whole year

How Consumer Lending makes money, and why a controls office matters to that.

  • Skills shown
  • Organisational/departmental strategy
  • Business Model
  • Financial strategy
  • CSR and sustainability strategy
  • Curiosity and strategic thinking

My first rotation, June to December 2025

Incident Management: sixteen people in four areas covering reporting, playbooks, incident readiness and regulatory compliance. I started in playbooks and moved to reporting.

My second rotation, January to June 2026

A move to a different Chief Controls Office and a new department. Control Design and Optimisation oversees change and IT systems risks and controls across Consumer Lending. I worked mainly on the IT systems side, looking after the risk profile for each product. I also supported the Homes side with its risk controls.

Lloyds Banking Group is one of the UK’s largest banking groups. Its brands include Lloyds Bank, Halifax, Bank of Scotland and Scottish Widows, and its purpose is Helping Britain Prosper.

Consumer Lending is the Group’s lending business for personal customers, from credit cards and personal loans to car finance and mortgages. Through Lloyds Bank, Halifax, Bank of Scotland and MBNA it is the UK’s largest credit card provider. Its Transport business includes Black Horse and Lex Autolease (Exhibit 2.1).

Most of its income is interest on that lending. What puts the income at risk is often operational: a process that harms customers, or a supplier failure that stops a product working (Exhibit 2.2).

A Chief Controls Office works inside the business, in the first line of defence. It helps risk owners run their controls and deal with incidents. My two rotations were in two different Chief Controls Offices, so the second was a move into a new department rather than a new team. Risk challenges that work as the second line, and Internal Audit checks it as the third (Exhibit 2.3). Incident Management, my first team, handled the incidents themselves (Exhibit 2.4).

Two pieces of regulation sit behind this work. The FCA’s Consumer Duty expects banks to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, and the UK’s operational resilience rules expect them to keep important services running when something breaks. The Group’s charge for historic motor finance commission arrangements shows what it costs when customer outcomes go wrong.

In July 2026 the Group set out Accelerate 2030. It aims to bring the cost-to-income ratio below 45% by 2030, from a target of below 50% for 2026, and to lift return on tangible equity to around 20%. Consumer Lending is also being merged with Consumer Relationships into one Consumer business. Exhibit 2.5 shows where my own work met the Group’s priorities.

What I learned

When I started I knew my own tasks well and the business around them less well. The Reflection Day feedback made that clear (page 11). Writing this page is how I closed the gap: I now know how Consumer Lending makes its money and where my work protected it.

What I would do differently

Learn how the business makes its money in my first month, before the work, rather than after the Reflection Day.

Where I used it next

In August 2026 I completed a recorded business-case task for a bank’s campus programme, using the same kind of reasoning (page 12).

Sources: Lloyds Banking Group half-year 2026 results and Accelerate 2030 targets, reported by AJ Bell; the Consumer restructure, reported by FStech; Lloyds’ tokenised deposits transaction, reported by FinTech Futures; the Crisis partnership page; Lloyds careers adverts describing Consumer Lending (2024 and 2025).

3Finding my feet

First rotation, from June 2025

Learning how a sixteen-person incident team worked, then leading my first project inside it.

  • Skills shown
  • Leading a professional team
  • Managing people and resources effectively
  • Workforce planning (delegation of tasks)
  • Innovation, development of new ideas and contingency planning
  • Ability to communicate clearly, concisely and professionally in writing
  • Appreciation of multiple perspectives
  • Demonstrating professional standards of behaviour and use of best practice within the organisation

My part

  • Completed the mandatory and team training, and booked an introductory call with every team member
  • Owned the playbooks and how-to guides, and linked them across the team’s SharePoint sites
  • Led the merge of two SharePoint sites into one, from a team survey to a working trial
  • Got the draft approved by all four general managers before building it
  • Scheduled colleagues by skill and assigned the tasks at regular project meetings

Why it mattered

Two sites meant two places to look during a live incident. One site put the playbooks and the on-call contacts in the same place.

My first month was training and conversations. I booked a call with every member of the team, and each one walked me through their area. By the end of the month I knew who to call for what, which made the rest of the year easier.

Under my first manager I owned the production of playbooks and how-to guides: the documents the team follows when an incident is live (Exhibit 3.1). I mapped each one and linked it to the right SharePoint site.

That exposed a bigger problem. The team had two SharePoint sites. One served Bronze incident management, with the playbooks and the on-call rota. The other served incident readiness, with the contacts and the spreadsheets for calculating an incident’s impact on each product. I was asked to lead the merge.

I sent the team a survey on what they used and what they would drop, and drafted a structure from the answers. All four general managers approved the draft before anything was built. I then scheduled colleagues according to their skills and handed out tasks at regular project meetings until a working site was on trial with the team. A round of updates followed (Exhibit 3.2).

My toolkit at this point

Before and after my first months, rated out of five

SharePoint
ServiceNow

What I learned

As the newest person in the team I couldn’t tell anyone what to do. Getting the four general managers to approve the draft first meant nobody had to be persuaded later.

What I would do differently

Start a log of my own deliverables in week one. I only began one, the brag document, in my second rotation.

Where I used it next

I ran the IP swap and my first team’s Christmas meeting in the same order: agree the plan, then build it (page 9).

4Paper to digital

First rotation, 2025

Carried forward from page 3: map the people before the work.

Turning a supplier failure into one view of how every Consumer Lending product was tracking against the Group’s paper-reduction targets.

  • Skills shown
  • CSR and sustainability strategy
  • Financial strategy
  • Articulating and translating vision into operational strategies
  • Developing and managing complex relationships across diverse stakeholders
  • Negotiation and influence
  • Ability to present information to a range of audiences

My part

  • Led the Printing & Mail initiative
  • Contacted every relevant product area by call or email, and got their latest paper and mail data
  • Built a tracker of each product against the Group’s targets
  • Shaped the story with my manager and presented it to the Managing Director of the Chief Controls Office

Why it mattered

Paper and post cost money and carbon, and the mail failure exposed the supplier risk as well. Leadership needed one honest view of each product against targets the Group had already set.

When a third-party supplier failed to deliver the bank’s post because of production problems, it was logged as a major incident. It added urgency to a shift that already made sense: digital letters cost less than paper ones and leave the bank less exposed to a single supplier.

I contacted every relevant product area, from credit cards and loans to transport and homes. Where I could I got people on a call, and where I couldn’t I emailed. Some of them were very senior. With their data I built a tracker of each product against the Group’s targets (Exhibit 4.1).

With my manager I turned the numbers and the conversations into a story, then presented it to the Managing Director of the Chief Controls Office (Exhibit 4.2). My manager told me afterwards that she was impressed by the confidence and professionalism I showed with very senior stakeholders.

What I learned

Senior people want to see where things stand and what to do next. Building the story with my manager before the meeting taught me to put the conclusion first.

What I would do differently

Share the tracker with each product area as well as with the Managing Director, so every team could see where it stood.

Where I used it next

The incident pack on page 5 and my risk owner packs on page 7 both open with the answer.

5The spike

First rotation, later in 2025

Carried forward from page 4: lead with the conclusion.

Finding out why moderate incidents with a key supplier doubled in one quarter, and learning to ask for help sooner.

  • Skills shown
  • Critical and analytical thinking
  • Ability to access, analyse and synthesise information
  • Ability to use computer programmes efficiently and effectively
  • Problem solving abilities
  • Ability to communicate clearly, concisely and professionally in writing
  • Self-management (managing expectations)
  • Reflective and learning mindset

My part

  • Sent the weekly note on the team’s work to the Chief Operating Office director
  • Owned part of the Consumer Lending Power BI dashboard and automated its morning refresh
  • Extracted the incident data from ServiceNow and built structured datasets in Excel
  • Traced the doubling to a card-scheme migration
  • Presented the findings to the Chief Operating Office director as a pack

Why it mattered

Moderate incidents still cost money and can reach customers. Tracing them to one cause let the business fix the cause rather than chase each incident.

Later in my first rotation I moved to the reporting team. Each week I sent the Chief Operating Office director a note on what the team had done (Exhibit 5.1). I also owned part of the Power BI dashboard that reported every incident the team managed. I kept its data current and removed the manual steps so it refreshed by itself every morning. When a number looked wrong I traced it back to ServiceNow and corrected it there.

Then moderate incidents with one of our third-party suppliers doubled from one quarter to the next (Exhibit 5.2). I had to learn ServiceNow properly first, including how incidents were categorised across the business. I pulled the records into structured datasets in Excel and worked through them until the pattern pointed to one cause: a large card-scheme migration (Exhibit 5.3). I built a pack for the Chief Operating Office director showing where incidents correlated and which areas to act on.

The feedback that changed how I work

My toolkit at this point

Before and after the reporting team, rated out of five

ServiceNow
Power BI
Excel

What I learned

I lost time trying to solve it alone. Asking early protects the deadline, and the quickest route to an answer is often a ten-minute conversation.

What I would do differently

Raise the first blocker within a day. I spent days working alone before the feedback made me change.

Where I used it next

Regular check-ins are how I kept up with same-day deadlines on the Homes work in my second rotation (page 7).

6The pitch

2025 to April 2026

Carried forward from pages 3 and 5: find the people who know, and ask early.

An eight-week sprint that took me from knowing nothing about tokenisation to a winning proposition for UK farmers, presented to the Group COO and CTO.

  • Skills shown
  • Innovation, development of new ideas and contingency planning
  • Sales and marketing strategy
  • Business Model
  • CSR and sustainability strategy
  • Curiosity and strategic thinking
  • Creative skills and abilities in work and approaches to working
  • Ability to present information to a range of audiences
  • Effective team working and networking
  • Leading a professional team

My part

  • Selected from more than 70 applicants for an eight-week programme of 27, one of three placement students
  • Learned tokenisation from scratch through weekly sessions with subject-matter experts
  • Studied how tokenisation had been used in markets abroad and adapted it into a proposition for UK farmland
  • Ran sessions with the Aspire network to gather the customer insight behind the proposition
  • Researched the Group’s commitments to farmers so the pitch spoke to its own priorities
  • Produced a short AI video of UK farmers with Sora 2
  • Built the pitch materials as Business Lead

Why it mattered

Our team won first place. The proposition went to the Group COO and CTO, then to the CEO of Scottish Widows and Insurance, Pensions & Investments, who approved it for the prototype phase. By April it had been cleared to continue to September.

The brief was to design an investment proposition that let several investors fund one borrower through fractional ownership of real-world assets. My feature team, Blockchain 2.0, built a tokenised solution on distributed ledger technology (Exhibit 6.1). I worked on the business side, and I started the eight weeks knowing nothing about tokenisation.

Exhibit 6.2 shows how the sprint ran. Each stage gave me something I needed for the next one.

The UK problem we chose was farmland. When we built the proposition in 2025, the government planned to cap full inheritance tax relief on farms at £1 million from April 2026, and farming families feared having to sell land to pay the bill. Our proposition let a family raise money by selling tokenised fractions of its land to investors, so it could keep the farm (Exhibit 6.3). The customer sentiment we gathered through the Aspire network backed the idea.

To make the pitch land inside Lloyds, I researched what the Group had already committed to farmers. It describes itself as the UK’s largest lender to farming and offers finance to help farmers move to regenerative practices. Presenting the proposition as another way to support farmers kept it inside the Group’s own priorities.

Sora 2 was not yet available in the UK, so I worked with a contact in the US to produce a short video. It shows UK farmers on their land, voiced by people I know, talking about the pressure the tax change put on their families and how selling a fraction of the land could keep the farm in the family (Exhibit 6.4).

The Group was testing tokenisation itself at the time. In January 2026 it completed the UK’s first gilt purchase using tokenised deposits on a public blockchain.

In week 8 we met in person for the first time, in Manchester, to plan the final pitch (Exhibit 6.5). We won first place, then presented in person to the Group COO and CTO in London in January 2026 (Exhibits 6.6 and 6.7). In April my line manager wrote the programme up for a Consumer Lending leader (Exhibit 6.8), and the programme lead told the team the proposition was going ahead (Exhibit 6.9).

In December 2025 the government raised the cap to £2.5 million, which shrank the number of families the proposition was built for. That shapes what I would do differently.

At a separate innovation day I pitched a proposition with a group of placement students to the director of the credit cards and transport business (Exhibit 6.10).

What I learned

Each stage of the sprint fed the next. Listening to customers before building the pitch made the difference, because it gave the technology a problem to solve.

What I would do differently

Test the proposition against a change in policy. The December 2025 change cut the number of estates facing a higher bill, so I would build the case on more than one need, such as succession planning or funding investment on the farm.

Where I used it next

I learned from the experts before presenting on indicators in my second rotation (page 7). At the Reflection Day I told this story as “we”. I now tell it as what I did (page 12).

Sources: the farm inheritance tax change and its revision, reported by Gravita (December 2025) and Money to the Masses (January 2026); Lloyds and farming, reported by Farming.co.uk; Lloyds’ tokenised deposits transaction, reported by FinTech Futures.

7Decision-ready

Control Design and Optimisation, January to June 2026

Carried forward from page 5: regular check-ins when the pace is fast.

Helping risk owners act on clearer information, from which indicators to keep to what each product’s risk profile looked like.

  • Skills shown
  • Effective decision making
  • Critical and analytical thinking
  • Proposing and implementing change
  • Leading and managing change
  • Ability to present information to a range of audiences
  • Self-management (stress tolerance, prioritisation of tasks)

My part

  • Presented my hackathon team’s ideas on indicators to the Consumer Lending Chief Controls Office
  • Joined the Indicator Working Group, deciding which indicators to keep, fix or retire and benchmarking industry approaches
  • Checked whether Homes controls carried the right type and execution labels, and recommended corrections
  • Produced data packs for Homes risk owners as control lifecycles changed
  • My main role: looked after the IT systems risk profile for each product, presenting it to risk owners and at risk forums
  • Helped redefine how the team used Jira, and kept my manager updated through a brag document and compliance pack status updates

Why it mattered

Risk owners can only act on what they can read quickly. Clear indicators and correctly labelled controls mean risks are judged on accurate information.

For my second rotation I moved to a different Chief Controls Office and a new department: Control Design and Optimisation, which oversees change and IT systems risks and controls across Consumer Lending in line with the Group’s Risk Management Framework. I worked mainly on the IT systems side and also supported the Homes side.

Indicators were new to me when my hackathon team asked me to present our ideas on them to the Consumer Lending Chief Controls Office. That presentation earned me a place on the Indicator Working Group. It reviewed more than 1,200 indicators to decide which to keep, fix or retire, and benchmarked how the wider industry uses them (Exhibit 7.1).

On the Homes side, control lifecycles could change several times a day and requests landed with same-day deadlines. I gathered and presented data on Homes risk controls and produced packs for risk owners. I also checked whether each control carried the correct type and execution labels. Where they didn’t, I recommended corrections and built a visual showing where the inconsistencies clustered (Exhibit 7.2).

On the IT systems side, which was my main role, I looked after the risk profile for each product. I met risk owners regularly and presented each of them with their profile, at their own meetings and at risk forums (Exhibit 7.3). I also helped redefine how the team used Jira, which made our agile ways of working simpler to follow.

My toolkit at this point

Before and after my second rotation, rated out of five

Jira
Power BI

What I learned

When information changes several times a day, being useful means getting the right version in front of risk owners quickly. Waiting for a perfect answer helps nobody.

What I would do differently

Keep a record of which indicators I argued to retire and why. The reasoning would have made a stronger exhibit than a dummy matrix.

Where I used it next

I now open written answers with the conclusion and follow with the evidence (page 12).

8Finding a better way

Second rotation, 2026

Carried forward from page 3: rapport across teams, built one conversation at a time.

Getting past a reporting limit by reaching across teams, and helping my team use AI with judgement.

  • Skills shown
  • Vision and initiative
  • Identification of opportunities
  • Effective team working and networking
  • Assertiveness
  • Curiosity and strategic thinking
  • Ability to use computer programmes efficiently and effectively

My part

  • Spotted that the OpenPages data model held fields the standard reports didn’t show
  • Followed up a short conversation with a risk graduate from a virtual training session
  • Through him, set up a discovery call with the platform team to take it forward
  • Used Copilot daily and joined the Chief Controls Office’s Copilot working group
  • Tested the premium Copilot model and the open-source LLM Council project for team use

Why it mattered

Fuller reporting means risks are overseen on complete information. AI used with judgement frees time for the work that needs a person.

Standard reports from OpenPages, our risk platform, showed only part of the data. Working in the reporting layer, I noticed that the underlying data model held fields the interface didn’t surface (Exhibit 8.2). Better reporting was possible if we could reach them.

I didn’t know who could help, so I went looking. I had spoken briefly to a risk graduate during a virtual training session. I followed up afterwards, and through him arranged a discovery call with the platform team (Exhibit 8.1).

I brought the same habit to AI. I used Copilot every day to speed up analysis and sharpen my writing. In the Chief Controls Office’s Copilot working group I helped the team find better uses for it, and I showed colleagues features they hadn’t found. I also tested the premium Copilot model and the open-source LLM Council project to see what would work for the team.

My toolkit at this point

Before and after my second rotation, rated out of five

Copilot and AI tools

What I learned

The answer often sits with someone I haven’t met yet. Following up a short conversation put the problem in front of the people who could fix it.

What I would do differently

Write the reporting gap up as a one-page proposal before the discovery call, so the platform team had something to respond to.

Where I used it next

The OpenPages story became one of the examples I use in graduate video interviews (page 12).

9Leading without a title

December 2025 to April 2026

Carried forward from page 3: agree the plan, then build it.

Leading people who didn’t report to me, from a role-swap scheme for more than 30 placement students to a hackathon with Crisis.

  • Skills shown
  • Leading a professional team
  • Workforce planning (talent management)
  • Emotional intelligence
  • Engaging with all
  • Giving constructive feedback
  • Developing and managing complex relationships across diverse stakeholders (internal and external)
  • Creative skills and abilities in work and approaches to working
  • Appreciation of multiple perspectives

My part

  • As Aspire’s placement hub lead, helped organise the IP swap and structured how it would run
  • Brought the swap into the Chief Controls Office through the Grow & Deliver co-lab
  • Acted as the link between our hackathon team and the Crisis organisers
  • Organised and ran my first team’s Christmas meeting, including team awards I designed with AI
  • Ran team meetings and information panels with guest speakers in my second rotation

Why it mattered

More than 30 placement students saw another part of the Group. Teams under pressure had a reason to come together.

As Aspire’s placement (IP) hub lead I helped organise the IP swap with the other hub leads and structured how it would run. Between February and April 2026 more than 30 placement students swapped roles with someone in another part of the Group. In my second rotation I brought the same idea into the Chief Controls Office through the Grow & Deliver co-lab and led the organising until I left.

At the Rethinking the Future of Giving hackathon, part of the Group’s partnership with Crisis, I was a brand ambassador. I was the link between our team and the organisers from Crisis and the Group. I guided the team and gave them feedback as they built a proposition for how people donate to and engage with charity through the Group (Exhibit 9.1).

In December I took on my first team’s Christmas meeting. I organised a Secret Santa for the evening before, at the team dinner, then ran the day itself with guest speakers and an energiser. I closed it with team awards I designed with AI and handed out after a secret vote (Exhibits 9.2 to 9.4). In my second rotation I kept running team meetings and information panels, bringing in guest speakers from across the business.

When I left my first team they sent me a goodbye board and a gift in the post (Exhibit 9.6).

What I learned

Without a title, people follow a clear plan and a reason to care. Recognising people in small ways did as much for the team as the projects did.

What I would do differently

Run a short survey after the IP swap, as I did before the SharePoint build, to show what people got from it.

Where I used it next

This year I applied to project-manage a student consulting team at Lancaster.

10Four reviews

September 2025 to June 2026

Carried forward from every chapter so far: act on feedback before the next review.

My Performance Passport, rated with my line manager every quarter, and what moved each strength.

  • Skills shown
  • Self-awareness (identification of own strengths and weaknesses)
  • Reflective and learning mindset
  • Motivation, productivity and drive to succeed
  • Self-management (resilience)
  • Effective team working and networking
  • Assertiveness

Every quarter my line manager and I rated me against the seven strengths in Lloyds’ Performance Passport. Lower is stronger, and 1 means above expectations. The passport sits on Lloyds systems, so Exhibit 10.1 recreates my four reviews.

Six of the seven strengths reached 1 by June. Explanation and Counterpoint were the last to get there, in my final quarter, and Ownership stayed at 2. Exhibit 10.2 sets out what moved each one.

Each review ended with what to work on next, and I took it into the following quarter. With six of seven strengths above expectations, my line manager referred me to the Reflection Day. What went wrong there was how I presented my year (page 11).

What I learned

Feedback every quarter moved six strengths to the top score. Ownership, the one that stayed at 2, is what I most need to take into a graduate role.

What I would do differently

Write down the one thing to change after each review. I acted on the feedback, but I have no record of it, and this portfolio would have used one.

Where I used it next

A short list of priorities, agreed with my manager each quarter (page 13).

11The setback

June 2026

Carried forward from page 10: six of seven strengths above expectations.

The Reflection Day, where I was not put forward for the graduate programme despite strong scores, and what the feedback told me.

  • Skills shown
  • Self-awareness (identification of own strengths and weaknesses)
  • Reflective and learning mindset
  • Self-management (resilience)
  • Ability to use verbal communication effectively
  • Assertiveness

This was the moment I learned most from, so I have worked through it with Gibbs’ reflective cycle (Exhibit 11.1).

On 25 June, the day before my last day, I wrote to the director to ask for honest feedback (Exhibit 11.2). She replied the same afternoon (Exhibit 11.3). Her four points to improve were the clearest feedback I had all year.

What I learned

Being good in the room is not the same as telling a clear story about yourself. I had the evidence and didn’t use it.

What I would do differently

Prepare the interview around my own impact, with the numbers I could stand behind, instead of scripting the presentation alone.

Where I used it next

Every application and video interview since (page 12).

12What I did with it

June to October 2026

Carried forward from page 11: an action plan.

Turning the Reflection Day feedback into how I tell my story in graduate applications and video interviews.

  • Skills shown
  • Reflective and learning mindset
  • Motivation, productivity and drive to succeed
  • Ability to communicate clearly, concisely and professionally in writing
  • Ability to use verbal communication effectively
  • Self-management (prioritisation of tasks and time management)
  • Self-awareness
  • Demonstrating professional standards of behaviour and use of best practice within the organisation

Exhibit 12.1 sets out every piece of developmental feedback I had during the year, what I did about it and where to see the result.

For written applications I now use one structure (Exhibit 12.2). It answers the storytelling point directly. Each paragraph does one job, and every claim is backed by a story of mine. The values step works the way the brand stage of the pitch did: I find out what the firm says it cares about before I write a word.

The elevator pitch needed the most work. In June the panel heard someone interested in finance and people. Exhibit 12.3 shows how I answer “why you?” now.

Since leaving Lloyds I have completed nine recorded video interviews for graduate and internship roles in banking and consulting. Several are still open, and one firm turned me down after the video stage, so the work isn’t finished. Lloyds pointed me to its standard graduate route and I have applied through it.

I hold my CV to the same standard as my answers. Where I can’t confirm a number I leave a gap to fill, rather than estimate one.

That last point is the one I am still working on. I lost one application by missing an assessment deadline, which is that feedback in practice. Every application and deadline now sits in one tracker, and I narrowed my search to two lanes, with finance and banking first and consulting second. CFA Level I study and my final year still compete for the same hours.

What I learned

Feedback only counts once it changes what I do. Writing each change down is what made it stick.

What I would do differently

Apply to fewer firms and prepare each one better, which is the fewer-priorities lesson again.

Where I used it next

Chapter 13 sets out how I will carry these changes into a graduate role.

The year in summary
